# Radiation therapy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Radiology > Radiation therapy*

[Original Article Link](/library/L50wkg)

---

## Summary

Radiation therapy is a nuclear medical treatment that employs <u>ionizing radiation</u> to kill abnormal cells or control their growth. It is one of the three main approaches to the treatment of <u>malignant tumors</u> alongside <u>chemotherapy</u> and <u>surgery</u>, but can also be used to treat noncancerous diseases such as benign <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>Cushing disease</u>, <u>Dupuytren contracture</u>, and <u>plantar fibromatosis</u>. Radiation therapy is typically employed as a supplement to other treatments and rarely represents the sole approach. There are three forms of radiation therapy: <u>external beam radiation therapy</u> (teletherapy), which involves <u>irradiation</u> from an external source; <u>unsealed source radiotherapy</u> (<u>systemic radioisotope therapy</u>), which involves the administration of <u>radiopharmaceuticals</u> that accumulate in target tissues and irradiate these internally; and <u>sealed source radiotherapy</u> (<u>brachytherapy</u>), which involves the implantation of radioactive material beside or within the tissue to be <u>irradiated</u>. The type of radiation therapy employed depends on the disease and the specific type of cancer being treated. Radiation therapy can be employed curatively (i.e., to kill the diseased tissue completely) or palliatively (e.g., to shrink a <u>tumor</u>, control its growth, or relieve symptoms caused by a <u>tumor</u>). Palliative indications include bone <u>pain</u>, spinal cord and nerve compression, and <u>hemostasis</u>. As with all medical use of <u>ionizing radiation</u>, the <u>radiation dose</u> should be maintained as low as reasonably achievable (<u>ALARA principle</u>) and appropriate safety measures should be observed to minimize <u>carcinogenic</u> effects.
